newsitem.title: FRANCE: Britain likely to join single currency - EU head.
newsitem.headline: Britain likely to join single currency - EU head.

text.p: Britain will likely eventually be forced to bow to pressure from its own business and financial community to join the planned single European currency, European Union president Jacques Santer predicted on Thursday.
"If the CBI (Confederation of British Industry) and the City ask the government to join, I do not see any British government refusing," Santer told journalists at a dinner.
So far, both Britain's ruling Conservatives and the opposition Labour party have adopted a wait-and-see attitude toward joining European economic and monetary union (EMU).

While some smaller British firms oppose monetary union, there are fears in the City of London and among big business that the country could forfeit its role as Europe's leading financial centre if it exercised its "opt-out" from the single currency. Prime Minister John Major negotiated the opt-out for Britain on monetary union in 1991.

The CBI, the country's leading business federation, has been a strong advocate of Britain joining the single currency but there are divisions in both main parties about whether the country should participate.
Santer indicated, however, that it was unlikely that Britain could be among the first wave of entrants into monetary union due to start on January 1, 1999.

"It has always been our interpretation of the provisions of the (Maastricht) treaty that a member state must participate for two years in the European monetary system" to join a single currency. "You only have to do the calculation," he said.

Santer added measures had been discussed to link the currencies of those inside monetary union and those outside to ensure stability after the single currency came into effect but that no country could be forced to take part.

He rejected suggestions by some critics that European Union members were taking short cuts to meet the deficit reduction criteria in a final sprint to qualify for a single currency and was unconcerned about recent German grumblings.

He said the EU's approval Thursday of the controversial use by France of a 37.5 billion franc transfer payment from France Telecom to cut its 1997 deficit was approved by its statistics agency Eurostat "on a neutral basis" as conforming with EU accounting rules.
German Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher had attacked the EU decision as encouraging "other countries which seemingly do not fulfill the criteria."
But Santer said that when the issue surfaced at an EU ministerial-level meeting attended also by the Bundesbank last month "there was no German reaction."

He said that in any event, the ultimate decision on which countries could join would be taken in 1998. This would give political leaders a chance to review not only 1997 budgetary performances but budget plans for 1998.
Santer reiterated he believed the march to a single currency was "irreversible" and said the number of countries qualifying to join in the first round should be between five and nine.
